title: Administrative, Clinical, and Management Functions

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Categorize common medical office tasks as administrative, clinical, or management functions.
- Describe the boundaries between entry-level administrative and clinical responsibilities.
- Recognize that clinical tasks are performed under supervision and within scope of practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Administrative work is like the office's calendar keeper — someone has to keep track of who is coming in and when, so everyone is on time and nothing gets missed.

### Question 2

Registering a new patient is like signing up for a library card — you need the person's name, address, and details before they can borrow books, so everything is ready when they arrive.

### Question 3

If two people are accidentally invited to dinner at the same time, the polite fix is to call one and pick a new time — not to squeeze both at one chair.

### Question 4

A reminder call is like a gentle nudge saying, 'Don't forget your visit tomorrow,' so fewer people forget to come.

### Question 5

If a friend cancels plans, you might invite someone else who was waiting for a spot — the office does the same with its waiting list.

### Question 6

If someone yells 'fire,' you don't put them on a waiting list — you call for help right away. Serious chest pain is the same kind of signal to get help fast.

### Question 7

Registration is like filling out the top of a form with your name, birthday, and address — the basic facts the office needs to know who you are.

### Question 8

If you get a new library card number, you update your account so books get checked out to you — the office updates the insurance card the same way.

### Question 9

When you move, you tell people your new address so your mail arrives — the office updates the chart for the same reason.

### Question 10

Check-in is like the front door: first you confirm you're on the list, then you make sure your contact details are right before going in.

### Question 11

If a friend is upset about waiting, the kind thing is to say 'I'm sorry you've waited' and help — not to argue or walk away.

### Question 12

Before mailing a package, you check the address is right so it arrives — reviewing a claim is checking it's complete so it gets paid correctly.

### Question 13

Think of coding like a puzzle where every piece must be present — the assistant makes sure all the pieces (the documentation) are there so the picture is correct.

### Question 14

If a letter is returned for a missing stamp, you add the stamp and send it again — you don't throw the letter away.

### Question 15

A copay is like paying for a bus ticket before you ride — you pay your share at the start, not a year later.

### Question 16

If a friend asks about a tricky receipt you don't understand, you ask someone who knows instead of making up an answer.

### Question 17

An EHR is like a well-organized notebook of a patient's health that the whole care team can share, so everyone is on the same page.

### Question 18

A chart is like a diary of care — you write down exactly what you saw and did, right away, not what you guess should be there.

### Question 19

You wouldn't hand someone's diary to a person who just claims to be their friend — the office checks permission first before sharing health details.

### Question 20

Writing down what happened right away is like taking a note while you still remember it — waiting makes details fuzzy.

### Question 21

A tidy, up-to-date record is like a clean desk — you can find what you need fast without mistakes.

### Question 22

Fixing a mistake in a record is like crossing out a wrong answer with one neat line and writing the right one — you keep the old line so everyone sees what changed.

### Question 23

Vital signs are the body's 'check engine' lights — temperature, heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure tell you how the engine is running.

### Question 24

98.6°F is the body's normal 'just right' temperature, like the comfortable setting on a thermostat.

### Question 25

Measuring blood pressure is like reading a scale — you stand still and level so the number comes out right.

### Question 26

You can feel your heartbeat's rhythm at the wrist, like tapping a rhythm on a tabletop.

### Question 27

If a fire alarm rings, you don't pretend it's silent — you tell someone. An unusual blood pressure is a signal to tell the clinician.

### Question 28

Writing down a measurement you didn't actually get is like writing a wrong answer in a test on purpose — it makes everything that follows wrong.

### Question 29

Rooming a patient is like welcoming a guest: say hello, make sure it's really them, show them in, and then get the things you need.

### Question 30

A person's weight is their private number — you write it down quietly and correctly, like keeping a friend's secret.

### Question 31

Asking why someone came to the doctor is like asking a friend 'What's wrong?' so you know how to help.

### Question 32

Preparing the room between patients is like resetting the table between dinner guests — clean surfaces and fresh supplies each time.

### Question 33

If a friend suddenly looked very sick, you wouldn't leave them alone — you'd stay and call for help fast.

### Question 34

Helping during an exam is like being a good helper in the kitchen — you hand the cook what they need and write down the recipe as they go.

### Question 35

Passing a tool is like handing scissors to a friend handle-first — you do it safely so no one gets hurt.

### Question 36

Helping someone into position is like helping a grandparent settle into a chair — slow, gentle, and with a kind explanation.

### Question 37

Medical asepsis is like sweeping to reduce dust; surgical asepsis is like making a room completely dust-free for a very delicate job.

### Question 38

If you've never driven a car, you wouldn't just hop in and try — you'd say you need lessons first.

### Question 39

Labeling a specimen right away is like writing your name on your lunchbox — it makes sure the right thing goes to the right person.

### Question 40

A specimen is like food that must be kept just right until it's cooked — stored and delivered carefully so it doesn't spoil.

### Question 41

The doctor is like the chef who picks the recipe; the assistant follows the recipe carefully to prepare the ingredients.

### Question 42

If a package has the wrong address, you stop and fix it rather than mailing it and hoping for the best.

### Question 43

A waived test is like a simple recipe the trained team can follow at the office — easy, but you still follow the instructions.

### Question 44

Giving a shot is like being allowed to drive — you need the law, a license (training), and permission, not just a busy day or a wish.

### Question 45

If you've never learned to swim, you don't jump into the deep end — you tell someone who can help.

### Question 46

Medicine is like a prescription recipe — you only give it when the doctor orders it and you've been taught how, and you always write it down.

### Question 47

Passing along a refill request is like delivering a note to the teacher — you deliver it, but the teacher decides the answer.

### Question 48

An assistant works like a team player who follows the coach (the clinician or manager) rather than making the big calls alone.

### Question 49

When you're worried about something, you tell the right grown-up in charge — not gossip about it or keep it secret.

### Question 50

A review is like a coach watching your practice to help you get better, not to make you feel bad.

### Question 51

Just because a teammate asks you to do something doesn't mean you're allowed — you check the rulebook first.

### Question 52

Managing supplies is like keeping a pantry stocked — enough of what you need, fresh, and nothing wasted.

### Question 53

A par level is like the line on a gas gauge that tells you it's time to refill before you run out.

### Question 54

First-in, first-out is like drinking the milk that expires soonest so it doesn't go bad.

### Question 55

Vaccines are like food that must stay cold — if the fridge is too warm, you tell someone and follow the plan, not pretend it's fine.

### Question 56

If the cookie jar count doesn't match the log, you tell an adult right away rather than rewriting the number.

### Question 57

Compliance is like following the rules of a game even when no referee is looking.

### Question 58

Safety compliance is like following the safety rules in a science lab — labeling, washing, and using the right containers every time.

### Question 59

Procedures are like a recipe the whole kitchen follows so every dish turns out safe and the same.

### Question 60

If you see a puddle on the floor, you wipe it up or tell someone so no one slips — you don't wait for a fall.

### Question 61

Improving is like fixing a leaky faucet — first you admit there's a drip, then you can fix it.

### Question 62

Administrative tasks are the 'paperwork and phones' side of the office, like being the front-desk helper.

### Question 63

Clinical tasks involve touching or checking the patient's body and health, like taking a temperature or blood pressure.

### Question 64

Management work is like being the organizer who keeps the shelves stocked and the rules followed.

### Question 65

Some jobs are like being both the person who greets a guest and the one who writes down their order — two jobs at once.

### Question 66

Being cross-trained is like being able to both cook and run the cash register — you help wherever you're needed.

### Question 67

The assistant is like the helper who gathers the ingredients, while the doctor is the chef who decides the meal.

### Question 68

The assistant can deliver the note but only the doctor signs the prescription — that's the boundary.

### Question 69

The physician is like the captain who decides the course; the assistant follows the captain's directions to help the crew.

### Question 70

The rulebook (state law) says what helpers are allowed to do, and the boss and doctor work within that book.

### Question 71

When you're not sure a move is allowed in a game, you ask the referee — you don't just play and hope.

### Question 72

Being new on a team means showing up on time, being polite, and being ready to learn — not running the whole show.

### Question 73

A credential is like a badge that shows you've learned the skills — CMA and CMAA are the badges for medical assistants.

### Question 74

The CMAA is like a certificate in running the front desk, while a clinical certificate is about helping with patient care — some people earn both.

### Question 75

Continuing education is like updating the apps on a phone — it keeps your knowledge working with the latest changes.

### Question 76

When a sports team is behind, players help each other within their own positions — not grab someone else's job or storm off.

### Question 77

If a player doesn't show up, the whole team struggles — a medical office is the same, and patients are counting on everyone.

### Question 78

You wouldn't use a power saw you've never seen without learning first — you'd ask someone to show you.

### Question 79

You can hand someone a school handout, but you let the teacher answer the hard questions — the assistant does the same with health information.

### Question 80

Taking a history is like writing down exactly what a friend tells you, without adding or leaving things out.

### Question 81

When someone asks a health question you're not trained to answer, you pass the question to the doctor rather than guessing.

### Question 82

Writing in a chart is like a scientist's notebook — you write what you actually saw and measured, not your guesses.

### Question 83

When many things need attention at once, you handle the most important one first and let people know you'll be right with them.

### Question 84

Clinical tasks are about the patient's body and health; administrative tasks are about schedules, forms, and bills.

### Question 85

Lifting with your legs and keeping your back straight is like how you'd lift a heavy box safely — bend your knees, not your back.
